To read and understand a simple internship contract.
Florence, January. The Ernesto cooperative, with its new analysis machine, needs a collaborator. Karl, the former apprentice from Malta, comes from Rome for an interview with Giulia and Chiara.
Karl, thank you for coming. Do you already know what it's about?
More or less. It's a six-month internship, isn't it?
Exactly. You would deal with the new analysis machine. The work consists of preparing the samples and reading the results.
I know it well. In Malta I used it more than two hundred times.
We know. And that's exactly why we thought of you. But you would have to give up a semester at university.
I've already thought about it. Professor Ruggeri says an internship is worth more than six exams. And then I can take part in the online courses.
The pay isn't high. It also depends on how many clients come.
It doesn't matter. I want to take advantage of this opportunity. It's not every day you get to work in Florence.
Do you realise how much work there will be? Two Mattia Preti paintings, twenty Tuscan churches and a fourteen-year-old boy who asks questions all day long.
Davide? I'll take care of him. In Malta he used to ask me the same questions on the phone.
Then that's fine for us. We trust you.
Welcome to the Ernesto cooperative, Karl. We're counting on you.

The machine arrived on 10 January, in a wooden crate as big as a fridge, on a van that couldn't get into via Maggio. Four people unloaded it, with the help of Rocco and two of his bricklayers, and carried it into the workshop one centimetre at a time, the way you carry an old painting. When it was installed, in the corner where Bellini's table had stood for forty years, Chiara looked at it with a mixture of love and terror. "Very nice," she said. "Now someone has to know how to use it." Matei and Giulia looked at each other. In Malta, Karl had used it. They had looked at the results.

The cooperative now had a new and pleasant problem: too much work. The contract with the Co-Cathedral in Valletta for the two Mattia Preti paintings began in March. Twenty Tuscan churches, after an article by Mancini, had already asked for their paintings to be analysed. And the city council, at Councillor Conti's suggestion, had entrusted the workshop with the restoration of a small Annunciation in the church of San Felice. Three partners were no longer enough. They needed someone to take care of the machine full-time. And the only one who really knew it was in Rome, studying art history with Professor Ruggeri.

Giulia called Karl one January evening. Karl answered from the library, whispering, as always. When Giulia explained what it was about, there was a silence so long that she thought the line had dropped. "Karl? Are you there?" "I'm here," he replied, in a strange voice. "I was just thinking. Two years ago I was a boy from Malta preparing glues on scaffolding. Now you're asking me to come to Florence to work in Ernesto Bellini's workshop. I realise it's not a joke, right?" Giulia laughed. "It's not a joke," she said. "But first you have to do an interview. With Chiara. And Chiara never jokes."

Karl arrived in Florence the following Saturday, on the first train from Rome, in a jacket and tie, with a CV printed on thick paper and a folder full of photos of the restoration in Malta. Davide was waiting for him at the station, because nobody had managed to stop him. They hugged like two brothers who hadn't seen each other for years, although they had never met in person and had only talked on the phone. Davide took him to the workshop by the longest route, across the Ponte Vecchio, past the trattoria and Guido's new shoemaker's, explaining everything like a tour guide.

In front of the trattoria, Davide stopped and pointed at the brass plaque next to the door. "We saved this one," he said proudly. "I mean, Pietro's grandmother. I mean, everyone." Then he pointed at the small plaque from 1966, higher up, blackened with time. "And this one shows how high the water came. My grandfather was here, with his shovel." Karl looked up at the plaque, then at the first-floor windows, then at the sign of Guido's shoemaker's, further on. "In Malta," he said quietly, "people told me Florence is a museum. They were wrong. It's a home." Davide thought for a moment, then wrote the sentence in his notebook. "I'll give this one to Pietro," he said. "For the diary. He collects the right sentences."

The interview lasted two hours. Chiara had prepared a list of handwritten questions and asked them one after another, without smiling. What exactly did the work he had done in Malta consist of? Which analyses had he dealt with? Had he ever noticed a machine error? How would he react if a client insisted on a wrong result? Karl answered calmly, in almost perfect Italian, with the Maltese accent that made everything a little musical. When he didn't know something, he said so. Chiara noted everything down. Giulia, sitting next to her, noticed that Chiara had stopped looking at the list after the fifth question. It was a good sign.

Then came the hard part: the conditions. Chiara explained them to him without sweetening them. It was a six-month internship, with modest pay, which depended partly on how many clients came. Karl would have to give up a semester at university, move to Florence, find a room to rent in a neighbourhood where rents, as everyone knew, were very high. "Do you realise what we're asking of you?" said Chiara at the end. "It's not a gift. It's hard work, poorly paid, in an expensive city." Karl looked her in the eye. "I realise," he replied. "And that's exactly why I want to do it."

Before giving him an answer, Chiara gave him one last test, which wasn't written on the list. She took him to the big table, where there was a small fifteenth-century panel with a thin crack near the Madonna's face, and asked him what he thought of it. Karl looked at it for a long time, without touching it, with his hands behind his back, as Bellini used to. Then he said that, in his opinion, before dealing with the crack you had to understand what it depended on: humidity, an old restoration or the wood itself. "I wouldn't trust my first look," he said. "I'd do an analysis." Chiara nodded slowly. It was exactly what she would have said. From his corner, Bellini, who was pretending to read the newspaper, raised his thumb without being seen.

The problem of the room was solved by Graziella, as always without anyone asking her. On the second floor of the building in via Maggio, after the agreement with Arno Living, there were six flats for residents at capped prices. One had just been vacated by a student who had gone back to Puglia. Graziella went to talk to the administrator, then to Valeria, then to the administrator again, and after three days Karl had a room with a window onto the courtyard, two hundred metres from the workshop, for a rent which, said Valeria, "hasn't been seen in Florence since 1990". In return, Karl had to promise just one thing: to eat at the trattoria at least three times a week.

The contract was written by Valeria, who now dealt with all the cooperative's paperwork on Saturday mornings. It was the first employment contract in the history of the workshop, which in a hundred years had passed from grandfather to father, from father to son, from master to apprentice, always with a handshake. Valeria read it aloud, at the trattoria, in front of everyone, on the evening before the signing. "The intern will deal with pigment analyses and the maintenance of the machine," she read. "He will take part in restorations under the supervision of the partners. He may take advantage of the workshop library and of Ernesto Bellini's diaries, which must be handled with gloves."

Bellini, from his table, raised a hand. "May I add an article?" he asked. Valeria nodded. Bellini took the contract, took out a pen and at the bottom, under the last article, wrote in his neat handwriting: "Article 9. The intern must answer all of Davide's questions, even the silly ones. Especially the silly ones. Because that's how you learn." Davide protested that he didn't ask silly questions. Karl laughed and said he accepted article nine without discussion. Valeria added it to the official contract, in bold, and said it was the most important article of all.

The signing took place the next day, in the workshop, next to the new machine. Karl signed with an ordinary pen. Then Giulia, Matei and Chiara signed for the cooperative, one after another. And at the end, against all the rules, Bellini asked to sign too, "as a witness". He signed with Ernesto's tiny brush, as he had signed the handover of the workshop in December. Nobody protested. Then Chiara shook Karl's hand and said the sentence she had been preparing for days, which came out with her voice slightly broken: "Welcome to the Ernesto cooperative. We're counting on you."

That evening Karl phoned his mother, in Malta, from the new room with the window onto the courtyard. He told her everything: the interview, the contract, article nine, the room, the trattoria. His mother listened without interrupting, then asked him a single question, in Maltese: whether he was eating enough. Karl laughed and told her that, according to his unwritten contract with Signora Graziella, he had to eat at the trattoria at least three times a week, and that the risk, if anything, was the opposite. His mother was silent for a moment. Then she told him she was proud of him, and that his grandfather, who had been a fisherman in Marsaxlokk, would have been happy to know that a grandson worked with his hands, even if with a brush instead of a net.

The first weeks weren't easy. Karl had to get used to everything: the cold of Florence in January, so different from Malta's; Graziella's dialect, which he didn't understand; the bicycle traffic in via Maggio; and above all article nine. Davide arrived at the workshop every afternoon at half past three, straight out of school, with a list of questions written in his notebook. Why did lapis lazuli blue cost so much? How did the machine manage to tell a seventeenth-century pigment from a nineteenth-century one? What would happen if it analysed ribollita? Karl answered everything, patiently. Even the last question.

To answer the last question, in fact, Karl did something nobody expected. One evening, after closing time, he asked Graziella for a spoonful of ribollita "for scientific reasons". Graziella looked at him suspiciously, but gave it to him. Karl prepared a sample, put it in the machine and waited an hour. The result, printed on a sheet, said: black cabbage, cannellini beans, Tuscan bread, extra virgin olive oil, tomato, carrot, celery, onion. And an unidentified substance, two per cent. Karl took the sheet to Graziella. "What's this two per cent?" he asked. Graziella smiled and handed the sheet back. "That," she said, "is the secret. And not even your machine will ever manage to discover it."

Davide stuck the sheet in his sketchbook, with the caption above it "Analysis of the ribollita — 98% science, 2% Grandma". Pietro, when he saw it, photographed it for his diary. And Mancini, who was passing by the trattoria for dinner, saw it stuck on the fridge and published it the following Sunday on the culture page of the "Gazzetta", with a short article entitled "Science surrenders to ribollita". The next day three restaurants phoned the workshop asking to have their dishes analysed. Chiara answered them all, politely, that the cooperative dealt with paintings, not cooking. But she added their numbers to the client list, "you never know".

In February the first samples arrived from the Tuscan churches. Karl analysed them day and night, with Davide keeping him company in the afternoon and Lupino sleeping at his feet in the evening. In three weeks he analysed thirty-two samples from eleven different churches. In two cases he discovered that the paintings had been repainted in the nineteenth century with the wrong colours. In one case, in a small country church near Siena, he discovered under an eighteenth-century Madonna the traces of a much older pigment, from the fourteenth century. When Giulia saw the results, she stayed silent for a long time. Then she told Karl, as Bellini had told her years before: "You know how to look. The rest can be learned."

That discovery made it into the "Gazzetta", then into a national newspaper, then into an art history journal. Professor Ruggeri, from Rome, called Karl to congratulate him and then Giulia to complain. "You've stolen my best student," he said. "Nevertheless, I realise he's learning more there than here. Tell him that, when he finishes the internship, he does his degree thesis with me. On that Madonna from Siena. I won't take no for an answer." Giulia passed the message on to Karl, who blushed to his ears, just as Davide blushed. Matei, looking at the two of them, said the workshop was becoming a factory of shy geniuses.

One evening at the end of February, Pietro found Karl and Davide sitting together on the workshop steps, in the cold, looking at via Maggio. Davide was asking his umpteenth question: whether Karl, after the internship, would go back to Malta or stay in Florence. Karl thought for a long time. "It depends," he said in the end. "On what?" asked Davide. "On many things. On work. On my thesis. On my mother, who asks me every day when I'm coming back." He paused. "But above all it depends on one thing. Whether I manage to discover what the two per cent in the ribollita is." Davide burst out laughing. "Then you'll stay here forever," he said. "Grandma will never tell anyone."

Pietro sat down with them. For a while none of the three spoke. From the trattoria, fifty metres away, came the noise of pots and Graziella's voice humming Viorica's lullaby, with the wrong accent. Further on, in Guido's shoemaker's, the light was still on. On the first floor of the building, behind the window of the little room, you could see Giulia's shadow putting Viola to bed. "You know what?" said Pietro in the end. "Two years ago this street was about to be sold. Now there's a historic trattoria, a shoemaker, a cooperative, a Maltese intern and an apprentice who draws balance sheets." Davide nodded. "And a boy who writes everything in the diary," he added.

That night Pietro opened the black notebook and wrote the date. Then, below, he looked for a sentence to sum up those months and chose his words carefully, as he had learned. "The workshop no longer depends on one person. Many people take care of it: three partners, an intern, an apprentice, a Saturday councillor, a retired professor who signs with a brush. Each one counts on the others. Nobody gives anything up. And everyone takes advantage of the ribollita." He reread it and thought that Grandpa Aldo, who never got a preposition wrong, would have been pleased. Then he added, in small letters, below: "I realise this sentence is too long. But I'm fond of it."

The next day, at breakfast, Graziella found on the kitchen table a sheet folded in four, in Karl's handwriting. It was written in slightly formal Italian, an intern's Italian. "Dear Signora Graziella, thank you for the room, for the ribollita and for your patience with my Italian. I realise I've only just arrived, but I'd like to ask you something: could you teach me to make ribollita? I'm not asking for the two per cent. I'll settle for ninety-eight." Graziella read the note twice, then put it on the kitchen shelf, next to Pietro's cup and Viorica's photo. "Ninety-eight per cent can be done," she said, to no one in particular. "The rest, my boy, depends on you."
